title: Disintegration of the Soviet Union
tagline: The causes of the Soviet collapse — stagnation, Gorbachev’s reforms and rising nationalism — and its impact on the world.

overview.intro: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, one of the two superpowers that divided the world for four decades, dissolved in December 1991 without a decisive military defeat. This unit examines the causes of its disintegration — political and economic stagnation, the reforms of glasnost and perestroika, and the nationalism of the constituent republics — and its impact: the end of the cold war, the emergence of new states and the beginning of a unipolar moment in international relations.

facts.label: Timeline

facts.label: Reforms
facts.value: Glasnost (openness), perestroika (restructuring), demokratizatsiya and the renunciation of the Brezhnev doctrine.

facts.label: Nationalism
facts.value: The Baltic states led, followed by the Caucasus and Ukraine; the August 1991 coup accelerated the exit.

facts.label: Impact
facts.value: End of the cold war, fifteen successor states, arms control, and a unipolar distribution of power.

learningOutcomes: Describe the political and economic stagnation of the late Soviet Union.
Explain Gorbachev’s reforms and their unintended effects.
Assess the role of nationalism in the disintegration.
Explain the impact of the collapse on international relations.

blocks.text: The Soviet system reached the 1980s carrying problems it could no longer disguise. Economically, central planning had proved effective at mobilising resources for heavy industry and defence but poor at producing consumer goods, innovation and quality; by the Brezhnev years the growth rate had fallen to near zero, shortages were routine, and the shadow economy supplied what the planned one could not. Military spending absorbed a share of output that no economy could sustain indefinitely, and the war in Afghanistan from 1979 drained resources and morale while demonstrating the limits of Soviet power.

Politically the system had ossified. Authority was concentrated in an ageing leadership with little turnover, decision-making ran through a bureaucracy that concealed failure rather than correcting it, and the ideology that legitimated the state had lost the belief of many of its own citizens. The command structure that allowed rapid mobilisation also penalised the reporting of bad news, so the leadership was the last to understand the depth of the problem. The result was a society with high formal employment and low initiative, an empire held by loyalty bought through subsidy, and a political class with no mechanism for renewal short of crisis.

Arms spending unsustainable; Afghanistan a draining commitment

blocks.text: Mikhail Gorbachev became general secretary in 1985 with a diagnosis that the system required renewal rather than replacement. Perestroika restructured the economy by permitting limited private enterprise, cooperative enterprises and some managerial independence, on the reasoning that central direction had stifled initiative. Glasnost opened public discussion, released information about the past including the crimes of the Stalin period, and relaxed censorship, which allowed problems to be named publicly for the first time in decades. Demokratizatsiya introduced contested elections for a new Congress of People’s Deputies in 1989, and a new conception of commonwealth allowed the republics greater autonomy within a reformed union.

The reforms contained an internal contradiction that proved fatal. Glasnost released the demands that the system had suppressed — national, religious and economic — faster than perestroika could satisfy them, so the leadership faced an explosion of criticism while living standards fell rather than rose. The partial democracy introduced to reform the party gave nationalist and anti-Soviet candidates a platform, and the abandonment of the Brezhnev doctrine, which had promised to intervene to preserve socialism in the bloc, signalled to Eastern Europe and then to the republics that Moscow would not use force. Each step was designed to save the union; each step removed a prop that had held it up.

blocks.caption: The three reforms and their effects
rows: Revive the economy through partial markets
Shortages worsened; black market filled the gap
Renew the party through contested elections
Signalled that force would not be used

blocks.text: The Union was a federation of republics in name and an empire in structure, and the national question had never been solved, only managed. Once glasnost permitted organisation and speech, the republics moved in a sequence that began in the Baltic. Lithuania declared independence in March 1990, followed by the other Baltic states, and the Caucasian republics and the larger republics followed through 1990 and 1991. Ukraine’s declaration of independence in December 1991, confirmed by the referendum of 1 December 1991 with an overwhelming majority, made the union unsustainable, since without Ukraine the remaining union had neither the population nor the weight to hold together.

The attempt to preserve the union by force failed. In August 1991 hardliners detained Gorbachev and declared a state of emergency, but the coup collapsed within three days in the face of resistance in Moscow and the refusal of troops to fire, and it destroyed the credibility of the central institutions it claimed to save. Within four months the republics had declared independence in succession, and on 26 December 1991 the Soviet of the Republics formally dissolved the union. The transition was remarkably bloodless in the centre, though conflicts in the Caucasus and Central Asia were exceptions, and it left fifteen successor states with unresolved borders and large Russian-speaking minorities.

items: The Baltic states led the way with declarations from March 1990.
Ukraine’s December 1991 referendum made the union untenable.
The August 1991 coup intended to preserve the union destroyed its institutions.
Moscow did not use decisive force, which distinguished this collapse from imperial breakups elsewhere.
The result was fifteen states with unresolved borders and minority populations.

blocks.text: The first impact was the end of the cold war. With the sponsor gone, the communist governments of Eastern Europe fell in the autumn of 1989 through peaceful revolutions, Germany was reunified in 1990, and the division of Europe that had organised international politics since 1945 disappeared. Arms control advanced through the Treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe and the START agreements, while the ideological contest between the two systems ceased to be the organising principle of the system.

The second impact was a unipolar distribution of power. The United States emerged as the only superpower, with the capacity to project force globally and no peer competitor, which shaped the decade through interventions, alliance management and the spread of free-market prescriptions to the successor states. The third impact was on the states of the former union themselves: they faced the tasks of nation-building, market reform and border settlement, and Russia inherited the nuclear arsenal and the seat at the table while losing the standing that had accompanied superpower status. For international relations as a discipline the collapse revived arguments about whether the balance of two powers had been stabilising, and the conflicts that followed in the Caucasus supplied evidence for those who thought it had.

questions.explanation: The introduction of contested elections for a Congress of People’s Deputies in 1989 gave opponents a platform.

questions.prompt: State four causes of the disintegration of the Soviet Union.
questions.answer: Four causes are: economic stagnation, with growth near zero, chronic shortages and consumer goods of poor quality; the unsustainable burden of defence spending and the war in Afghanistan; the reforms of glasnost and perestroika, which released demands faster than they could be satisfied and gave opponents a platform; and rising nationalism in the constituent republics, which spread from the Baltic declarations of 1990 to Ukraine’s referendum of 1991. The ageing leadership and loss of ideological belief are also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each cause must be explained as a mechanism rather than named.

questions.prompt: Explain how Gorbachev’s reforms contributed to the breakup they were designed to prevent.
questions.answer: Perestroika was meant to revive the economy, but partial liberalisation disrupted the planning system without creating functioning markets, so shortages worsened and living standards fell precisely when the leadership needed public support. Glasnost was meant to expose bureaucratic failure so it could be corrected, but by allowing open discussion it released the national, religious and political demands the system had suppressed for decades, and information about the crimes of the past further eroded the legitimacy of the party that had inherited them. Demokratizatsiya introduced contested elections in 1989, which were intended to renew the system but gave nationalist and anti-Soviet candidates a lawful platform from which to attack it. Finally the renunciation of the Brezhnev doctrine removed the guarantee of force that had held the Eastern Europe bloc together and showed the republics that secession would not be met with intervention. The contradiction was therefore structural: reform required criticism, and criticism required a legitimacy the system could no longer supply, so each measure removed a prop that had supported the union while adding nothing that could replace it.
questions.explanation: The answer must identify the paradox — reform releasing faster than it delivers — and trace each reform to its specific effect.

questions.prompt: Assess the impact of the disintegration of the Soviet Union on international relations.
questions.answer: The first and most immediate impact was the end of the cold war. The rivalry between the two superpowers had organised alliances, intervention and arms competition since 1945, and with the sponsor of the eastern bloc gone the communist governments of Eastern Europe fell in the autumn of 1989 through largely peaceful revolutions, Germany was reunified in 1990, and the division of Europe disappeared. Ideology ceased to be the axis of the system, and arms control advanced through the Treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe and the START agreements at a pace the stalemate had never allowed. The second impact was a unipolar distribution of power: the United States emerged as the only superpower, with the capacity to project force globally and no peer competitor for roughly a decade, which shaped the 1990s through intervention, alliance management and the spread of market prescriptions. The third impact fell on the states of the former union itself, which had to build nations and institutions from scratch, settle borders, manage Russian-speaking minorities and undertake rapid market reform, while Russia inherited the nuclear arsenal and the seat at the table but lost the standing that had accompanied superpower status. The fourth impact was theoretical and regional: conflicts in the Caucasus and Central Asia showed that the collapse was not uniformly peaceful, and the record revived the argument about whether the balance of two powers had been more stabilising than the disorder that replaced it. The judgement that best fits the evidence is that the disintegration removed the constraint that had disciplined the system, producing both the liberalisation of Europe and a series of regional conflicts that bipolar rivalry had previously suppressed.
questions.explanation: Full marks need at least three impacts each explained with evidence, plus a judgement that weighs the benefits against the instability.

questions.prompt: Was the Soviet Union destroyed by Gorbachev’s reforms or by the system they attempted to save? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: The case against Gorbachev is that his decisions released the forces that dissolved the union. Glasnost permitted publication of the crimes of the Stalin era and open attacks on the party’s record, which destroyed the legitimacy on which obedience rested; demokratizatsiya gave Baltic nationalists and anti-Soviet candidates a lawful platform in 1989; economic liberalisation disrupted the planning system without producing working markets, so shortages worsened and the population lost patience with a leader who promised improvement; and the renunciation of the Brezhnev doctrine told both Eastern Europe and the republics that force would not be used. On this reading a leadership that had chosen reform over repression, and a particular sequence of reforms, produced the outcome. The case that the system itself was finished rests on deeper evidence. Economic growth had fallen to near zero before Gorbachev took office, because central planning was structurally poor at quality, innovation and consumer supply, and no plausible reform could reconcile the party’s control with the information a market requires. The legitimacy of the system depended on performance and belief, and both had eroded under Brezhnev: the leadership was ageing, the ideology was widely disbelieved, and the empire in Eastern Europe was held by subsidy that the economy could no longer afford. Nationality grievances dated not from 1986 but from the union’s founding and had been suppressed rather than resolved, so any relaxation of control would have released them, as it had in 1956 and 1968 when force still held. The strongest synthesis is that the system determined the outcome once reform began: a regime that could only survive by coercion or by economic success was losing the second, and Gorbachev’s attempt to find a third way required precisely the openness and political participation that a nationally composed federation could not survive. The counterfactual that tests the judgement is telling — a leadership that chose force, as in China, preserved the state, which shows that choice mattered — but the Chinese case also shows that economic contradiction and nationality remained unresolved, so the argument is between a proximate and a structural cause rather than between cause and no cause.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both cases argued from specific evidence, the counterfactual addressed, and a reasoned conclusion distinguishing the proximate trigger from the structural cause.
